analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax on the largest inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently repeal the estate tax died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the federal estate tax, the tax owed by estates of people who die leaving more than roughly $11.4 million per person. The bill was introduced with 9 House Republican sponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a vote when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021. The bill also keeps stepped-up basis, meaning heirs would never pay income tax on investment gains that accumulated during the original owner's lifetime.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the very largest estates. The federal estate tax in 2019 applied only to estates above roughly $11.4 million per person (about $22.8 million per married couple), so repeal would deliver large tax savings to a small number of ultra-wealthy families and their heirs, with no benefit for the vast majority of households whose estates fall below the threshold and owe nothing. Estate planning, trust, and wealth advisory professionals would also benefit from continued demand for sophisticated avoidance strategies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently repeals chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code, the federal estate tax, for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2018, so heirs of large estates would owe no estate tax.

The bill explicitly retains stepped-up basis at death, meaning inherited assets keep their tax basis reset to their value at death; heirs can sell later without ever paying income tax on the appreciation that built up during the original owner's lifetime.

Supporters of estate tax repeal generally argue it spares family farms and small businesses from liquidation to pay the tax; under 2019 law, though, the roughly $11.4 million per-person exemption already exempted nearly all of them from owing any estate tax.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Repealing the estate tax would permanently eliminate a tax paid only by the estates of very wealthy people, forcing the government to replace that revenue through other taxes, more borrowing, or cuts to public services. Retaining stepped-up basis means heirs of large estates could still sell inherited assets without ever paying income tax on the decades of gains that built up during the original owner's life.

drawbacks.text: The bill's cost falls on the federal Treasury, not just the wealthy: the estate tax raises tens of billions of dollars a year from the largest estates, so repealing it permanently adds to deficits or forces higher taxes and lower services for everyone else.

By keeping stepped-up basis at death, the bill means the largest unrealized capital gains would never be taxed at all — no estate tax, and no income tax when heirs sell — a permanent escape hatch for wealth built up over generations.

The tax applies only to the very largest estates — above roughly $11.4 million per person in 2019 — so the bill delivers nothing to the vast majority of families while cutting taxes exclusively for the wealthiest heirs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to the heirs of multimillion-dollar estates, since the 2019 exemption already shielded estates below roughly $11.4 million per person. The costs — lost revenue that must be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or service cuts — are spread across everyone else. Because the bill also preserves stepped-up basis, the largest fortunes could pass entirely untaxed; the benefits and costs are sharply lopsided toward the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert E. Latta introduced the bill on January 11, 2019 with eight Republican cosponsors, to repeal the estate tax for estates of people dying after December 31, 2018.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced; that was its last action.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without ever receiving a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead: the estate tax, which is paid only by the largest estates, survived repeal. No one paid a price because the bill never reached a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the estate tax survives

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Repeal would exempt estates above roughly $11.4 million per person from the estate tax, directly reducing what the wealthiest families' heirs owe. The public's cost is the lost revenue, which must be made up elsewhere.

industries.industry: Estate planning, wealth management, and trust services
industries.note: By retaining stepped-up basis alongside repeal, the bill preserves the core of estate planning for large fortunes, keeping demand for services that structure inheritances to minimize tax.
